source_refs.note: Topic 22.3.2 with the pie chart, the x-axis data figure and error bars (PDF 199-203); the book's three charts are replaced by original charts from its data. The book's step 3 writes 'x 100' and degree values with '%' for the sector angles; the lesson uses x 360 and degrees.

blocks.text: A pie chart is a circular graph divided into sectors, each representing a proportion of the whole. The whole circle is 100%, or 360 degrees, and each sector's angle is proportional to its category's share. Pie charts suit categorical data as parts of a whole, such as types of cells, species distributions or survey responses.

items: Organise the data in a table of categories and frequencies.
Calculate each sector angle: (category value / total) x 360.
Draw a circle and, with a protractor, mark each angle in turn from a starting radius, using different colours.
Label each sector, add a legend if needed and give a descriptive title.

blocks.alt: A pie chart of the blood groups of 100 students: O 40% (the largest slice, red), A 30% (blue), B 20% (green) and AB 10% (yellow). A legend gives each group's number of students and its angle: A 108, B 72, AB 36 and O 144 degrees.
blocks.caption: Pie chart of blood types (original chart drawn from the book's data).
blocks.long_description: A pie chart shows parts of a whole: the whole circle is 100% or 360 degrees, and each sector's angle is its share times 360. For the 100 students, group A (30) gets 30/100 x 360 = 108 degrees, B (20) 72 degrees, AB (10) 36 degrees and O (40) 144 degrees; the angles add up to 360 degrees.

blocks.text: The x-axis is the horizontal line of a graph, usually used for the independent variable; the y-axis shows the dependent variable measured against it. In biology the x-axis often shows time, species or experimental conditions. To make the figure: identify the variables; choose the scale and range; label the axes with units; plot each pair of values; and, where useful, join the points with a line to show the trend.

In the book's example enzyme activity was measured at five temperatures: (5 C, 2), (10 C, 4), (20 C, 7), (30 C, 5) and (40 C, 3) micromoles per minute, with temperature on the x-axis and activity on the y-axis.

blocks.alt: A line graph titled The effect of temperature on enzyme activity. The x-axis is temperature from 0 to 45 C and the y-axis enzyme activity from 0 to 8 micromoles per minute. Points (5, 2), (10, 4), (20, 7), (30, 5) and (40, 3) are joined by a line that rises to a peak at 20 C and then falls.
blocks.caption: Enzyme activity against temperature (original graph drawn from the book's data).
blocks.long_description: In an x-axis data figure the independent variable, here temperature in degrees Celsius, is on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable, enzyme activity in micromoles per minute, on the vertical y-axis. Each pair of measurements is plotted as a point and the points are joined to show the trend: activity rises from 2 at 5 C to a maximum of 7 at 20 C and falls to 3 at 40 C. The temperatures are placed on a true scale, so the gap from 5 to 10 C is half the gap from 10 to 20 C.

blocks.title: Keep the scale true
blocks.text: The book says the temperatures can be evenly spaced because the intervals are similar, but they are 5, 10, 10 and 10 degrees apart. On a true scale, as drawn here, the 5 to 10 C gap is half the size of the others.

Error bars on a bar chart show the variability or uncertainty of the data behind each bar, how far the individual values typically lie from the mean shown by the bar. Range error bars run from the smallest to the largest value of a group. Standard deviation error bars extend above and below the mean by one or more standard deviations (mean plus or minus SD). A short horizontal cap is drawn at each end.

blocks.caption: Bean plant heights in three light conditions (book's data, cm)

blocks.alt: A bar chart of mean bean plant height under low, medium and high light: 10, 15 and 19 cm. Each bar has a black error bar with caps, from 9 to 11, 14 to 16 and 18 to 20 cm, the range of the three plants in each group.
blocks.caption: Mean plant heights with error bars (original chart drawn from the book's data).
blocks.long_description: Error bars show the variability of the data behind each bar. Here each bar is the mean height of three bean plants grown in low, medium or high light (10, 15 and 19 cm), and each error bar runs from the smallest to the largest value of its group (a range error bar). In this example the range is 2 cm for each group, so the bars also show the mean plus or minus 1 cm, which the book gives as about one standard deviation.

blocks.title: About the standard deviation here
blocks.text: The book gives SD about 1 for each group. With the chapter's formula (dividing by N = 3) the SD of 9, 10 and 11 is about 0.82; dividing by N - 1, as is usual for a small sample, gives exactly 1. The range error bars (plus or minus 1 cm) are exact.

blocks.prompt: Show that the blood-type angles add up to a full circle.

items: Pie: angle = share x 360; full circle 360 degrees.
X-axis figure: independent variable on x, dependent on y, true scale.
Error bars: range (min to max) or mean +/- SD, with caps.
